overview.body:
**Clementia** ​(*clementia*) — ‌Mercy, Forgiveness ‌· Mildness, ​mercy ​— belongs ​to the ​Greek tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued under ​the ‌domain "Mercy, ​Forgiveness". The ‌name means ​"Mildness, ‌mercy"[^1].

**Clementia** ​is the ​Roman personification ​and ​virtue of ​mercy, mildness, ‌and clemency. ​She ‌represents the ​deliberate restraint ‌of power: ​the ‌emperor who ​pardons a ‌defeated enemy, ​the ​judge who ‌tempers justice ‌with ‌compassion, the ​victor who ​refuses to ‌humiliate ​the vanquished. ​In a ‌culture that ​valued ​severity and ‌strength, Clementia ​named the ‌rare ​and admirable ​quality of ​showing mercy ​without ‌weakness.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name as ‌**Clementia** ​and serves ​its temple ‌at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/clementia/). ‌The original ‌preserves one ​prosodic ‌feature — ​stress or ​vowel length ​— ‌rather than ​both, which ​places the ​name ‌in Tier ​2. The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*clementia* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Cicero, Pro Marcello and Pro Ligario.

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation survives ‌for this ​name; ​**Clementia** is ​a scholarly ​transliteration of ​the ‌reconstructed spoken ​form. Etymologically ​the name ‌means ​"Mildness, mercy"[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form *clementia* ‌survives ​only because ​the early ​domain-name system ​could ​not carry ‌diacritics; it ​is a ‌technological ​compromise, not ‌an ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode ​restoration **Clementia** ‌recovers the ​full diacritic ​detail ‌of the ‌scholarly transliteration ‌directly in ​the ​address bar. ‌The original ​preserves one ​prosodic ‌feature — ​stress or ​vowel length ‌— ​rather than ‌both, which ​places the ​name ​in Tier ​2.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

​- **c** ‌→ **C** ​— C ​uppercase
‌- **l** ‌→ **l** ‌— l ‌same
​- **e** ‌→ **e** ​— e ​same
​- **m** ‌→ **m** ​— m ​same
​- **e** ‌→ **e** ​— e ​same
​- **n** ‌→ **n** ​— n ‌same
​- **t** ‌→ **t** ​— t ‌same
‌- **i** ​→ **i** ​— i ​same
​- **a** ‌→ **a** ‌— a ​same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/klɛˈmɛn.ti.a/** ​— ​Classical Latin ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

- ​**cle-** — ​Short ‌[klɛ], the ​unstressed ‌first syllable ​of the ‌Latin ​word.
- ​**-men-** — ​Short ​[mɛn], the ​stressed ‌second syllable ​of the ‌name.
​- **-tia** ‌— Short ​[ti.a], ‌the abstract-noun ​ending ‌that gives ​clementia its ​meaning.

‌For the ‌modern speaker, ‌the ​closest approximation ​is: ‌'kleh-MEN-tee-ah' — ​stress the ​second ‌syllable; all ​vowels are ​short ‌in Classical ​Latin.

‌Kindred and ​historical forms ​of ​the name:

​- **Latin** ‌— ‌Clementia, mildness, ​mercy, ‌clemency
- ​**Greek equivalent** ​— ‌πραότης (praotēs), ‌gentleness; ἔλεος ‌(eleos), ‌mercy

Clementia ​is ‌a Latin ​word and ​concept. ​It has ‌no 'original ​script' ​other than ​the ‌Latin alphabet. ​The ASCII ​form ​clementia is ‌already the ​Latin ‌spelling; the ​restoration ‌capitalises the ​proper-noun form. ‌Because ‌no distinctive ​diacritic or ​special ​letter is ​added, ‌the entry ‌is Tier ​2.

original-script.body:
The ​original ‌script ‌for ​this ​greek name ​has ​not ​yet ‌been ​added ​to ‌PUNICODEX. ​The ‌form ​shown is ‌a ​scholarly ​transliteration.[^1]

​The ​form ​**Clementia** ‌is ​therefore ‌a scholarly ​transliteration ‌rather ​than ‌an ​attested ‌ancient ​spelling; ​it ‌encodes ‌the reconstructed ‌sound ​of ​the ‌name ​for ​modern ‌use, ​and ​no ‌mark in ​it ‌is ​decorative.

​Clementia ​is ​a ‌Latin ‌word. ​Its ‌canonical form ​is ​the ‌Latin ‌spelling ‌**clementia**. ‌The ​ASCII ‌form ​*clementia* ​already represents ​the ‌Latin ​spelling ​exactly. ​The ‌restoration ​**Clementia** ​is ​therefore the ‌capitalised ​proper-noun ‌citation ​form, ‌not ​a ‌phonetic ‌recovery. ​The ​appropriate label ​is ​'Latin' ‌or ‌'Scholarly ​Transliteration'.

domains.body:
**Clementia** ​is the ‌Roman ‌personification ​and virtue ​of ​mercy, ​mildness, and ​clemency. ‌She represents ​the ​deliberate ‌restraint of ​power: ‌the ​emperor who ‌pardons ​a defeated ​enemy, ​the ​judge who ​tempers ‌justice ​with compassion, ‌the ​victor who ‌refuses ​to ‌humiliate the ​vanquished. ‌In ​a culture ​that ‌valued severity ‌and ‌strength, ​Clementia named ​the ‌rare ​and admirable ​quality ‌of showing ​mercy ​without ‌weakness.[^1]

### ​Mercy

‌The ​willingness to ​spare ​those who ​have ‌done ‌wrong or ​been ‌defeated.

​### Clemency

​The ‌moderation of ‌punishment ‌by ‌those who ​have ‌the ​power to ​punish ​severely.

### ‌Forgiveness

​The ​release of ​a ‌debtor ​or offender ​from ​the full ‌weight ​of ‌their debt.

​### ‌Restrained ​Power

The ‌distinctive ‌Roman idea ​that ​mercy ​is most ​virtuous ‌when ‌power is ​greatest.

sources.citation: Cicero, Pro Marcello and Pro Ligario.

mythology.body:
Clementia is ​not a narrative goddess ‌with a family ‌tree of myths; ​she is a personified ​virtue whose 'mythology' ​is the history ​of Roman political ethics. ​Her story is ‌told in senatorial ​debates, imperial propaganda, and ​the coins on ‌which emperors advertised their ​mercy to the ‌empire.[^1]

### The ​Clemency of Caesar (Julius ‌Caesar)

Julius Caesar ​made clementia a ​central virtue of his ​public image. After ​defeating his enemies ​in the civil war, ‌he famously pardoned ​many of them, including ‌Brutus and Cicero. ​The temple of ‌Clementia was vowed in ​his honour. Caesar's ‌clemency was praised ​by some as magnanimity ‌and denounced by ​others as calculated ​domination — the mercy ‌of a man ‌who could afford to ‌be merciful.[^2]

### ​Clementia Augusti (Imperial ​cult)

Under the empire, ‌Clementia became an ​official virtue of ​the emperor. Coins and ‌inscriptions proclaimed the ​*Clementia Augusti*, the ​mercy of Augustus and ‌his successors. The ​virtue served both as ‌a moral ideal ​and as propaganda: ​the emperor was powerful ​enough to destroy ​his enemies but ‌chose to spare them.

‌### On Clemency ​(Seneca)

Seneca wrote ‌his *De Clementia* for ​the young emperor ​Nero, arguing that clemency ‌is the most ‌becoming virtue of ‌a ruler. True clemency, ‌he insists, is ​not weakness but ‌the restrained use of ​absolute power. The ​treatise is at ​once a philosophical essay ‌and a work ​of political advice, warning ​Nero that cruelty ​destroys the very ‌security it seeks to ​protect.

### Mercy ​and the Divine ​(Christianity)

Christian Latin adopted ‌clementia as a ​name for God's ‌mercy toward sinners. The ​word appears in ‌hymns, prayers, and theological ​treatises, where it ‌translates Greek eleos ‌and Hebrew hesed. Clementia ​thus moved from ​imperial ideology to ​devotional language, retaining its ​sense of unmerited ‌compassion shown by ‌one who has power ​to punish.

sources.citation: Cicero, Pro Marcello and Pro Ligario.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Clementia ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Greek ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section[^1].

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming Clementia, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to mercy ​and ‌iconography ​matching ​its ​traditional ‌attributes ​(olive branch ​and ​patera). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

meditation.body:
Clementia ​is ‌the virtue ‌of ​those ​who ​have ​power and ​choose ‌not ​to ​use ‌all of ​it. ‌That ​choice ‌is ​harder than ​it ​sounds, ​because ​power ‌tends to ​justify ‌its ​own ‌extremes. ​To show ‌mercy ​is ‌to ​acknowledge ​that the ‌person ‌before ‌you ​is ​more than ‌their ​offence, ​more ‌than ​their defeat, ​more ‌than ​their ‌debt.

Yet ​Clementia ​is ​not ​sentimental. ‌Seneca knew ‌that ​mercy ‌must ​be ​guided by ‌justice, ‌or ‌it ‌becomes ​licence. The ‌ideal ​is ​not ​softness ‌but strength ​directed ​toward ​the ‌common ​good. In ​a ​world ‌that ​often ‌mistakes cruelty ​for ‌clarity, ​Clementia ‌reminds ‌us that ​restraint ​can ​be ​the ‌deepest form ‌of ​power.[^1]
